desc:
API documentation writing and developer guides decide whether outside developers connect to your API or give up. Ecom Swift LLC tests each endpoint and writes the quick start, examples and error guide that let a newcomer make a first call fast.

## What is API documentation?

API documentation is the manual for developers who want to use your API. It explains how to sign in, what each endpoint does, what to send, what comes back and what the errors mean. Good documentation also shows working examples that can be copied and run.

It is the first thing a developer reads and often the only thing. If it is unclear, they move on to a competitor or flood your support inbox.

## Why developers judge you by your docs

A developer evaluating your product has no time to guess. They open the docs, look for a quick start, try one call and decide within minutes whether the integration is worth their week. Missing parameters, outdated examples and vague error text all signal a product that is hard to use.

Strong docs also reduce your own workload. Questions that would reach your support or engineers are answered on the page. New team members learn the API from the same source customers use.

## How good docs change adoption and support

Documentation works as a sales tool and a support tool at once. A clear quick start shortens the time between signing up and the first successful call, which is when most developers form their opinion. Tested examples prevent the typical failure of copy-paste code that does not run.

Error guides cut tickets. When every error code has a cause and a fix, developers solve problems alone. Over time that frees your engineers from repeated explanations and lets partners go live without a long email thread.

## What useful API docs contain

- A quick start that reaches a first successful request in a few steps.
- An authentication guide covering keys, tokens and where to find them.
- A page for every endpoint with parameters, types and required fields.
- Request and response examples that were run against the real API.
- Examples in curl and the programming languages your users prefer.
- An explanation of every error code and how to fix it.
- Guides for common tasks, such as creating an order and then listing it.
- A changelog that tells developers what changed and when.
- A try-it panel generated from your OpenAPI file, in larger builds.

## How we write them

We read what exists, then test every endpoint ourselves, because untested docs are a risk. Where behavior differs from what the code comments say, we ask you which one is intended. We write in short, plain sentences with the same terms used everywhere.

Delivery depends on where your docs should live. The smaller package gives you Markdown files, the middle one adds a quick start, multi-language examples and a published page on your site, and the largest one adds a full docs site with a try-it panel, how-to guides, a changelog and a handover so your team can edit it later.

## Do and avoid

**Do:**
- Put the quick start at the top of the docs.
- Use real sample values that look like your data.
- Keep terms identical across every page.
- Update the changelog whenever the API changes.
- Have a developer outside your team follow the quick start.

**Avoid:**
- Copying the code comments word for word.
- Showing examples that were never run.
- Hiding the authentication steps deep in the docs.
- Explaining errors with only a status code.
- Letting the docs drift behind the API.

## Who it is for

A company launching a public API needs a docs site before the first outside developer arrives. A team that inherited an undocumented API needs someone to test it and write down what it really does. A product with a growing support queue about integrations needs better guides and error explanations.

## What we need from you

Send us access to a test version of the API, a sandbox key and any existing notes or OpenAPI file. If there is no OpenAPI file, we can work from the live routes. We use a developer or collaborator user and never need your passwords. Tell us who your readers are, so we pick the right language examples.
